newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: EU says Slovakia lacks rule of law and democracy.
newsitem.headline: EU says Slovakia lacks rule of law and democracy.

text.p: The European Union on Thursday warned Slovakia that it must strengthen its democratic process, including adherence to the rule of law, if Bratislava wants to be considered for EU expansion.

But EU External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek, visiting ahead of a final assessment next month of the country's eligibility to join the bloc, said there was no danger of the EU cancelling Slovakia's association agreement.

"I wish to convey...our concern that the rule of law and democracy do not yet appear to be sufficiently deeply rooted in Slovakia," van den Broek told a news conference at the end of a one-day official visit.

Van den Broek said he had held lengthy talks with Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar during which he presented the EU views. "We had a lengthy discussion which was useful even if we did not agree," van den Broek said.
"I made my plea that my comments should not be taken as a patronising diktat, but as an expression of concern of a friend who wants to see Slovakia become a member of the European family."

During his talks with Meciar, President Michal Kovac, parliamentary leaders from all parties and leading industrialists, van den Broek said concerns had been highlighted by events surrounding recent referendums.
Slovaks went to the polls in plebiscites last weekend on NATO membership and direct presidential elections, but the votes were declared void because ballot papers were invalid.
"All Slovakia's friends were appalled by the circumstances surrounding the invalidation of last weekend's referendum," van den Broek said.
"...when the judgement of the Constitutional Court and the position taken by the Central Referendum Commission were effectively ignored by the authorities," he added.

The twinned referendums were billed as a last chance for Slovakia, which has come under fire from the West for its lack of democratic reforms, to win an invitation to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in the first wave of new members.

Instead, voting degenerated into chaos highlighting a feud between Meciar and Kovac who had included a question about presidential elections on the ballot on the basis of a statewide petition, and prompted a boycott when it was struck off at the last moment.
The Central Referendum Committee declared the widely boycotted weekend referendum void and denounced ballot papers distributed by the Interior Ministry as a "massive swindle".
Van den Broek noted that the EU had over the past few years already expressed its deep concern about the stability of political institutions in Slovakia.

The EU expected Slovakia to send "clear and unambiguous signals" that it was fulfilling the political conditions for EU membership by the end of the year to retain its eligibility for admittance to the community.
These included adequate opposition representation in parliamentary committees and an improvement in the respect for and protection of minorities, van den Broek said.
The Commissioner said Slovakia's economic results were positive, but noted its low level of direct foreign investment which he also attributed to to the country's political environment.
